summary.text: The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, is a series of reactions that release the energy stored in nutrients through acetyl-CoA oxidation.
Its NADH is fed into oxidative phosphorylation, and the two closely linked pathways together oxidize nutrients to produce usable chemical energy as ATP.
In eukaryotic cells it occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and it connects carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Krebs cycle, Szent–Györgyi–Krebs cycle, TCA cycle

facts.label: Yield per pyruvate
facts.value: Three NADH, one FADH₂, and one GTP or ATP

facts.label: Enzymes involved
facts.value: Eight enzymes carry out the reactions

facts.label: Krebs's prize
facts.value: Hans Adolf Krebs received a Nobel Prize in 1953

items.prompt: The citric acid cycle can keep turning, round after round. What makes that possible?

options.label: The citrate is saved to start the next cycle
NADH loops back round to become the acetyl group
Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end of each turn
Carbon dioxide is fed back in at the last step

items.explain: At the end of each cycle the four-carbon oxaloacetate has been regenerated, and the cycle continues.

items.prompt: The citric acid cycle produces NADH. Where does that NADH go next?

options.label: Into oxidative phosphorylation, which makes ATP
Back into glycolysis to rebuild glucose
Out of the cell as a waste product
Into the first step to rebuild citrate

items.explain: The NADH generated by the cycle is fed into the oxidative phosphorylation pathway to generate ATP.

items.prompt: Two carbon atoms leave the cycle as carbon dioxide during one turn. Where do those carbons originate?

options.label: From the two-carbon group just added
From what was already oxaloacetate
From the water that the cycle consumes
From the NAD⁺ that gets reduced

items.explain: The carbons lost as CO₂ originate from what was oxaloacetate, not directly from the group donated by acetyl-CoA.

items.prompt: A bacterium has no mitochondria yet still runs the citric acid cycle. Where does it happen?

options.label: In the nucleus, using the nuclear envelope for the gradient
Inside a mitochondrion borrowed from another cell
In the mitochondrial matrix of its own cell
In the cytosol, using the cell surface membrane for the gradient

items.explain: In prokaryotes the reaction sequence is performed in the cytosol, with the proton gradient across the plasma membrane.

items.prompt: A student insists metabolites in the citric acid cycle must always follow one fixed route. What is wrong with that?

options.label: The route changes with each turn of the cycle
Only the first half of the cycle follows a fixed route
At least three alternative pathways of the cycle are recognized
Metabolites follow the route only in prokaryotes

items.explain: Even though it is branded a cycle, it is not necessary for metabolites to follow a specific route; at least three alternatives are recognized.

items.prompt: After several turns, some carbons from acetyl-CoA may never leave as carbon dioxide. Why?

options.label: Many cycle intermediates are used as precursors to build other molecules
They are locked inside NADH permanently
Acetyl-CoA stops entering after the first turn
Each is converted straight back at the same step

items.explain: Because of the cycle's role in anabolism, many intermediates are used as precursors for the biosynthesis of other molecules.

paragraphs.heading: What the cycle does
paragraphs.text: The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle, is a series of reactions that frees the energy held in nutrients by oxidizing acetyl-CoA. That energy becomes available as ATP. The cycle is named after citric acid, or citrate, which is used up and then made again each time around. Along the way it takes in acetate, carried as acetyl-CoA, and water, turns NAD⁺ into NADH and gives off carbon dioxide.

paragraphs.heading: A hub of metabolism
paragraphs.text: The cycle links the handling of carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Breaking down sugars, fats and proteins all yields acetyl-CoA, a two-carbon compound that enters the cycle. The cycle also supplies building blocks for certain amino acids, and the reducing agent NADH, for other reactions. Organisms that get energy by respiration, with or without oxygen, use it, while organisms that ferment use other pathways. Its central role suggests it was one of the earliest parts of metabolism.

paragraphs.heading: One turn of the wheel
paragraphs.text: Each turn starts when a two-carbon acetyl group moves from acetyl-CoA onto oxaloacetate, a four-carbon compound, making six-carbon citrate. Citrate then goes through a series of changes and loses two carboxyl groups as CO₂. By the end, oxaloacetate has been remade, ready for the next turn. Eight enzymes carry out the work. Oddly, the carbons given off as CO₂ come from what was oxaloacetate, not straight from acetyl-CoA.

paragraphs.heading: The energy payout
paragraphs.text: Each turn converts three NAD⁺ into NADH, one FAD into FADH₂, and one GDP plus inorganic phosphate into GTP. The NADH and FADH₂ then go to oxidative phosphorylation, which uses them to make energy-rich ATP. There, each NADH yields 2.5 ATP and each FADH₂ yields 1.5.

paragraphs.heading: Where it happens
paragraphs.text: In eukaryotic cells the cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix. In bacteria, which lack mitochondria, it runs in the cytosol instead. Their proton gradient for making ATP lies across the plasma membrane at the cell's surface, not across the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. Either way, the NADH the cycle makes feeds the electron transport pathway, and together these two closely linked pathways oxidize nutrients to give usable ATP.

paragraphs.heading: Who worked it out
paragraphs.text: In the 1930s Albert Szent-Györgyi established several of the cycle's parts by studying pigeon breast muscle. He won the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his findings on fumaric acid, one of its components. In 1937 Hans Adolf Krebs and William Arthur Johnson, working at the University of Sheffield, finally identified the full cycle. Krebs received the Nobel Prize for it in 1953, and the cycle is sometimes named after him. Working separately, German biochemists Carl Martius and Franz Knoop also identified the cycle in 1937.
